units.translation: a lock of hair as a thank-offering to Inachus, and this second one as a mourning offering
he gaped around my breast that nourished him

They say that the Greeks wore their hair long at all other times, but cut it in time of mourning; for then, having cut a lock, they dedicated it to Apollo the nourisher of youths and to the rivers. And this lock was the thank-offering according to Aeschylus, while the other was the mourning lock. They say that Theseus first began the cutting of the thank-offering lock. For having cut, they say, the front hair, he dedicated it to Apollo in Delos.

I have just ceased lamenting my own sorrows
who will bury him? who will lament him?

where Triclinius repeats the annotation of Thomas Magister: ἐθέρισεν, ἔκειρεν · κοινῶς δὲ ἔθριξεν, ἀφεῖλεν · ἀφ᾿ οὗ καὶ ἡ θρίξ. καὶ Εὐριπίδης [he reaped, he sheared; but commonly he cut hair, he took away; from which also comes θρίξ [hair]. And Euripides] (Or. 128) “ἴδετε παρ᾽ ἄκρας ὡς ἀπέθριξεν τρίχας” [see how he has cut the hair from the top]. ἀπέθρισεν [he cut off] has been restored to Euripides from inferior manuscripts, but rightly, as the verse of Helen 1188 teaches: κόμας σίδηρον ἐμβαλοῦσ᾽ ἀπέθρισας [having put the iron to your hair you cut it off], although in Hesychius is read ἀπέθριξεν: ἀπέκειρεν, ἀπέκοψεν [he cut off: he sheared, he cut].
he reaped, he sheared; but commonly he cut hair, he took away; from which also comes θρίξ [hair]. And Euripides
see how he has cut the hair from the top. he cut off
having put the iron to your hair you cut it off
he cut off: he sheared, he cut
and the lock of upright hair stands up
and may the white hair of my beard be destroyed
